lec05kp08-u01-p1-title.name: u01-p1-title
lec05kp08-u01-p1-title.text: The cost surface is a narrow valley: plain gradient descent takes 100 steps and swings from side to side

lec05kp08-u01-p1-bridge.name: u01-p1-bridge
lec05kp08-u01-p1-bridge.text: KP07 training took thousands of epochs, partly because gradient descent itself is slow. When it is slow, how exactly does it move?

lec05kp08-u01-p1-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp08-valley
lec05kp08-u01-p1-fig1.text: Contours of the narrow valley with the path of plain gradient descent: starting at (−4, 1) it swings along w₂ and needs 100 steps to reach the origin.

image.alt: Contours of the narrow valley with the path of plain gradient descent: starting at (−4, 1) it swings along w₂ and needs 100 steps to reach the origin.

lec05kp08-u01-p1-term:曲率.name: term:Curvature
lec05kp08-u01-p1-term:曲率.text: **Curvature**: how sharply the cost surface bends. Where the curvature is large, a small step changes the cost a lot.

lec05kp08-u01-p1-term:病態代價面.name: term:Narrow valley
lec05kp08-u01-p1-term:病態代價面.text: **Narrow valley (ill-conditioned surface)**: very large curvature in one direction and very small in another, so the contours are flat ellipses. Here $J=\tfrac12(w_1^2+20w_2^2)$: curvature 20 along $w_2$ and 1 along $w_1$.

lec05kp08-u01-p1-c1.name: u01-p1-c1
lec05kp08-u01-p1-c1.text: **Result**: from $(-4,1)$ with $\mu=0.08$, plain gradient descent needs 100 steps to reach $|w|<0.001$ (distance to the minimum $(0,0)$) and the path swings up and down along $w_2$.

lec05kp08-u01-p2-title.name: u01-p2-title
lec05kp08-u01-p2-title.text: The steep direction is multiplied by −0.6 each step and flips sign, the flat direction only by 0.92 and creeps

lec05kp08-u01-p2-bridge.name: u01-p2-bridge
lec05kp08-u01-p2-bridge.text: In the narrow valley plain gradient descent took 100 steps and swung from side to side. Which direction causes the swing?

lec05kp08-u01-p2-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp08-zigzag
lec05kp08-u01-p2-fig1.text: w₁ and w₂ over the first 15 steps: w₁ shrinks steadily by a factor 0.92 and w₂ shrinks with alternating sign by a factor −0.6.

image.alt: w₁ and w₂ over the first 15 steps: w₁ shrinks steadily by a factor 0.92 and w₂ shrinks with alternating sign by a factor −0.6.

lec05kp08-u01-p2-c1.name: u01-p2-c1
lec05kp08-u01-p2-c1.text: **The steep direction**: the gradient of $w_2$ is $20w_2$, so $w_2\leftarrow w_2-0.08\cdot20\,w_2=-0.6\,w_2$: it flips sign every step and shrinks only to 0.6 times.

lec05kp08-u01-p2-c2.name: u01-p2-c2
lec05kp08-u01-p2-c2.text: **The flat direction**: $w_1\leftarrow w_1-0.08\cdot1\cdot w_1=0.92\,w_1$: always the same direction and only 8% smaller per step, hence slow.

lec05kp08-u01-p2-c3.name: u01-p2-c3
lec05kp08-u01-p2-c3.text: **The dilemma**: $\mu$ must stay below $2/20=0.1$ or $w_2$ swings ever wider; with $\mu=0.12$ the norm $|w|$ exceeds $10^8$ after 60 steps. But such a small step makes $w_1$ slow.

lec05kp08-u01-p3-title.name: u01-p3-title
lec05kp08-u01-p3-title.text: Momentum: this step is α times the previous step plus the new gradient step

lec05kp08-u01-p3-bridge.name: u01-p3-bridge
lec05kp08-u01-p3-bridge.text: In the steep direction the gradient flips sign every step, so positives and negatives could cancel. How can each step remember the previous one?

lec05kp08-u01-p3-term:動量.name: term:Momentum
lec05kp08-u01-p3-term:動量.text: **Momentum**: gives the update inertia: besides the new gradient step, this step adds $\alpha$ times the previous step (momentum factor $\alpha$, 0.1 to 0.8 in practice).

lec05kp08-u01-p3-c1.name: u01-p3-c1
lec05kp08-u01-p3-c1.text: **Update rule**: $\Delta w(t)=\alpha\,\Delta w(t-1)-\mu\,g(t)$ with $g$ the gradient and $\mu$ the learning rate $\eta$ of KP06; $\alpha=0$ is plain gradient descent.

lec05kp08-u01-p3-c2.name: u01-p3-c2
lec05kp08-u01-p3-c2.text: **By hand** ($\mu=0.08$, $\alpha=0.6$): step 1 is $(0.32,-1.6)$; step 2 is $0.6\times(0.32,-1.6)-0.08\times(-3.68,-12)=(0.4864,\,0)$, so the two pulls on $w_2$ cancel exactly.

lec05kp08-u01-p4-title.name: u01-p4-title
lec05kp08-u01-p4-title.text: Momentum averages past gradients exponentially: a steady direction grows the step by 1/(1−α)

lec05kp08-u01-p4-bridge.name: u01-p4-bridge
lec05kp08-u01-p4-bridge.text: In step 2 the two pulls on $w_2$ cancel exactly. Unrolled over many steps, what is momentum computing?

lec05kp08-u01-p4-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp08-expo
lec05kp08-u01-p4-fig1.text: Bar chart of the weights 0.6^t and 0.8^t that shrink for older gradients; with a fixed gradient the total weight is 1/(1−α), 2.5 and 5 times.

image.alt: Bar chart of the weights 0.6^t and 0.8^t that shrink for older gradients; with a fixed gradient the total weight is 1/(1−α), 2.5 and 5 times.

lec05kp08-u01-p4-term:指數加權平均.name: term:Exponentially weighted average
lec05kp08-u01-p4-term:指數加權平均.text: **Exponentially weighted average**: the newest gradient weighs most and every older one is multiplied by $\alpha$ once more, weights $1,\alpha,\alpha^2,\dots$.

lec05kp08-u01-p4-c1.name: u01-p4-c1
lec05kp08-u01-p4-c1.text: **Unrolled**: $\Delta w(T)=-\mu\sum_{t}\alpha^{t}g(T-t)+\alpha^{T}\Delta w(0)$; the last term is near 0 after a few steps.

lec05kp08-u01-p4-c2.name: u01-p4-c2
lec05kp08-u01-p4-c2.text: **Faster when steady**: the total weight is $1+\alpha+\alpha^2+\cdots=1/(1-\alpha)$: 2.5 times for $\alpha=0.6$, 5 times for $\alpha=0.8$ (program check); alternating signs cancel.

lec05kp08-u01-p5-title.name: u01-p5-title
lec05kp08-u01-p5-title.text: Same start, same μ=0.08: momentum with α=0.6 turns 100 steps into 28

lec05kp08-u01-p5-bridge.name: u01-p5-bridge
lec05kp08-u01-p5-bridge.text: With a steady direction momentum enlarges the step, and when the sign flips it cancels the swing, like an exponentially weighted average of past gradients. Run for real, how far apart are the two paths?

lec05kp08-u01-p5-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp08-two-paths
lec05kp08-u01-p5-fig1.text: Two paths from the same start with the same μ=0.08: plain needs 100 steps and momentum with α=0.6 needs 28, with a faster-shrinking swing.

image.alt: Two paths from the same start with the same μ=0.08: plain needs 100 steps and momentum with α=0.6 needs 28, with a faster-shrinking swing.

lec05kp08-u01-p5-c1.name: u01-p5-c1
lec05kp08-u01-p5-c1.text: **The paths**: plain descent (red) swings up and down along $w_2$ many times; momentum (green) shrinks the swing faster and moves faster along $w_1$ too.

lec05kp08-u01-p5-c2.name: u01-p5-c2
lec05kp08-u01-p5-c2.text: **Steps**: to $|w|<0.001$, plain needs 100 steps and momentum 28 (program).

lec05kp08-u01-p5-c3.name: u01-p5-c3
lec05kp08-u01-p5-c3.text: **The price**: one more stored array for the previous update and one more knob $\alpha$ to tune.

lec05kp08-u01-p6-title.name: u01-p6-title
lec05kp08-u01-p6-title.text: α has a best value: 0.6 is fastest, α ≥ 0.9 is even slower than no momentum

lec05kp08-u01-p6-bridge.name: u01-p6-bridge
lec05kp08-u01-p6-bridge.text: Momentum with $\alpha=0.6$ turned 100 steps into 28 steps. Would a larger $\alpha$ be even faster?

lec05kp08-u01-p6-c2.name: u01-p6-c2
lec05kp08-u01-p6-c2.text: **Too large**: $\alpha=0.95$ needs 247 steps, slower than no momentum: too much inertia overshoots the valley floor and rocks like a pendulum before it stops.

lec05kp08-u01-p6-c3.name: u01-p6-c3
lec05kp08-u01-p6-c3.text: **In practice**: 0.1 to 0.8, the best value depends on the problem and must be tried; the source reports speed-ups of 2 times or more.

lec05kp08-u01-p7-title.name: u01-p7-title
lec05kp08-u01-p7-title.text: Adaptive learning rate: speed up 5% when better, brake 30% when worse

lec05kp08-u01-p7-bridge.name: u01-p7-bridge
lec05kp08-u01-p7-bridge.text: Momentum has a best value of $\alpha$, and a bad choice is slower than plain descent. The learning rate $\mu$ is the same: $\mu=0.02$ takes 411 steps and $\mu=0.12$ blows up. Can $\mu$ adjust itself?

lec05kp08-u01-p7-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp08-adaptive
lec05kp08-u01-p7-fig1.text: Semi-log curve of |w| against steps: plain μ=0.02 needs 411 steps, adaptive from 0.02 needs 61 and from 0.12 needs 95, and plain μ=0.12 quickly blows up.

image.alt: Semi-log curve of |w| against steps: plain μ=0.02 needs 411 steps, adaptive from 0.02 needs 61 and from 0.12 needs 95, and plain μ=0.12 quickly blows up.

lec05kp08-u01-p7-term:自適應學習率.name: term:Adaptive learning rate
lec05kp08-u01-p7-term:自適應學習率.text: **Adaptive learning rate**: adjust $\mu$ automatically from the ratio of the cost before and after: $J(t)/J(t-1)<1$ gives $\mu\times1.05$; above $1.04$ gives $\mu\times0.7$; otherwise unchanged.

lec05kp08-u01-p7-c1.name: u01-p7-c1
lec05kp08-u01-p7-c1.text: **Asymmetric**: slow growth when better, hard braking when worse. When the cost rises the step is rejected and momentum zeroed.

lec05kp08-u01-p7-c2.name: u01-p7-c2
lec05kp08-u01-p7-c2.text: **Result**: $\mu_0=0.02$: plain 411 steps, adaptive 61; $\mu_0=0.12$: plain blows up, adaptive converges in 95. $\mu_0=0.08$: 93 steps against 100.

lec05kp08-u01-p8-title.name: u01-p8-title
lec05kp08-u01-p8-title.text: quickprop jumps once per weight to the estimated parabola bottom: 5 steps on this quadratic

lec05kp08-u01-p8-bridge.name: u01-p8-bridge
lec05kp08-u01-p8-bridge.text: The adaptive learning rate brakes or speeds up by the ratio of the cost before and after, yet each step uses only the slope. Can two slopes estimate the valley floor?

lec05kp08-u01-p8-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp08-compare
lec05kp08-u01-p8-fig1.text: Steps of five methods: plain μ=0.02 411, adaptive 61, plain μ=0.08 100, momentum 28 and quickprop 5.

image.alt: Steps of five methods: plain μ=0.02 411, adaptive 61, plain μ=0.08 100, momentum 28 and quickprop 5.

lec05kp08-u01-p8-term:quickprop.name: term:quickprop
lec05kp08-u01-p8-term:quickprop.text: **quickprop**: weights are independent; the last two slopes estimate the parabola bottom and the weight jumps there: $\Delta w(t)=\alpha(t)\,\Delta w(t-1)$, $\alpha=\min\{g(t)/(g(t-1)-g(t)),\,1.75\}$.

lec05kp08-u01-p8-c1.name: u01-p8-c1
lec05kp08-u01-p8-c1.text: **Example** ($w_2$): step 1 goes $1\to-0.6$, slope $20\to-12$; $\alpha=-12/(20+12)=-0.375$, $\Delta=+0.6$: step 2 lands on 0; $w_1$ likewise, growth capped at 1.75.

lec05kp08-u01-p8-c3.name: u01-p8-c3
lec05kp08-u01-p8-c3.text: **But**: every slice here is a parabola, ideal for quickprop; real costs are not. The five step counts are in the figure.

lec05kp08-u01-p9-title.name: u01-p9-title
lec05kp08-u01-p9-title.text: Extension: quickprop is Newton's method in one dimension; on this quadratic full Newton needs one step

lec05kp08-u01-p9-bridge.name: u01-p9-bridge
lec05kp08-u01-p9-bridge.text: quickprop estimates the valley floor of each weight and jumps there. How does that relate to Newton's method?

lec05kp08-u01-p9-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp08-secant
lec05kp08-u01-p9-fig1.text: Parabola along w₂: an ordinary step from 1 to −0.6, then the slopes 20 and −12 give α=−0.375 and the next step lands on the minimum at 0.

image.alt: Parabola along w₂: an ordinary step from 1 to −0.6, then the slopes 20 and −12 give α=−0.375 and the next step lands on the minimum at 0.

lec05kp08-u01-p9-term:牛頓法.name: term:Newton's method
lec05kp08-u01-p9-term:牛頓法.text: **Newton's method**: use the curvature (the Hessian matrix $H$) to compute the valley floor directly: $\Delta w=-H^{-1}g$. A quadratic is solved in one step.

lec05kp08-u01-p9-c1.name: u01-p9-c1
lec05kp08-u01-p9-c1.text: **Here**: $H=\mathrm{diag}(1,20)$ and $\Delta w=-H^{-1}g=-w$, one step to $(0,0)$; the price is computing, storing and inverting the Hessian.

lec05kp08-u01-p9-c2.name: u01-p9-c2
lec05kp08-u01-p9-c2.text: **The family** (source): conjugate gradient, the Newton family, Kalman filtering and Levenberg–Marquardt, mostly needing the Hessian. Also delta-bar-delta: one learning rate per weight, grown when its gradient keeps its sign and shrunk when it flips.

lec05kp08-u01-p10-bridge.name: u01-p10-bridge
lec05kp08-u01-p10-bridge.text: Each weight's update rule can be rewritten on its own, even with its own learning rate. Take the momentum rule: given the first two steps, what are the gradient and the update of step 3?

lec05kp08-u01-p10-q1.name: u01-p10-q1
lec05kp08-u01-p10-q1.text: **Question 1**: after step 2 $w=(-3.1936,-0.6)$; what is the gradient $g=(w_1,\,20w_2)$?

lec05kp08-u01-p10-q3.name: u01-p10-q3
lec05kp08-u01-p10-q3.text: **Question 2**: what are the update $\Delta w(3)$ and the new $w$ after step 3?

lec05kp08-u01-p11-title.name: u01-p11-title
lec05kp08-u01-p11-title.text: Extension: worked solution of questions 1 and 2

lec05kp08-u01-p11-bridge.name: u01-p11-bridge
lec05kp08-u01-p11-bridge.text: The practice asked for the gradient, the update and the new $w$ of step 3. Worked out in full, what are the answers?

lec05kp08-u01-p11-a3.name: u01-p11-a3
lec05kp08-u01-p11-a3.text: **Check**: $w_2$ did not move in step 2, so its inertia is 0 in this step and the whole 0.96 of the gradient part becomes displacement.

steps.label: Speeding up backprop
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Main line 8 pages plus 3 extension pages (not timed). Self-study deck, English version. Made under CLARITY.md C12 to C18. Everything uses one narrow quadratic valley J=1/2(w1^2+20 w2^2) with start (-4,1); all step counts and paths were recomputed by a program, and this example was designed for this lecture to show the mechanisms (added); the source has its own interactive narrow-valley demo. Speaker notes are published with the file and contain no student numbers, grades or exam items.

steps.label: Narrow valley
steps.speakerNotes: KP07 training took thousands of epochs, partly because gradient descent itself is slow. This page first asks how it moves when it is slow. Two words first: curvature is how sharply the cost surface bends; a narrow valley has a very large curvature in one direction and a very small one in the other, so the contours are flat ellipses, which the source calls ill-conditioned, meaning the eigenvalues of the Hessian differ a lot. The example is J equal to one half of w1 squared plus 20 times w2 squared, start (-4, 1), learning rate 0.08. Plain gradient descent needs 100 steps to get the norm below 0.001, and the path swings up and down along w2. The next page asks why it swings.

steps.label: Why it swings
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said plain gradient descent takes 100 steps in the narrow valley and still swings. This page asks which direction causes the swing. The steep direction is w2: its gradient is 20 times w2, and after the update w2 becomes minus 0.6 times itself, so it flips sign every step and shrinks only to 0.6 times. The flat direction is w1: after the update it is 0.92 times itself, always in the same direction and only 8 percent smaller per step, hence slow. The dilemma is that the learning rate must stay below 0.1 or w2 swings ever wider; with learning rate 0.12 the norm exceeds 10 to the 8 after 60 steps. But such a small step makes w1 slow. The next page asks whether each step can remember the previous one so that the swinging part cancels.

steps.label: The momentum term
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page asked whether each step can remember the previous one so the swinging part cancels. This page is momentum: the update is alpha times the previous update plus minus the learning rate times the new gradient; alpha is the momentum factor, 0.1 to 0.8 in practice, and alpha equal to 0 is plain gradient descent. By hand with learning rate 0.08 and alpha 0.6: step 1 is (0.32, -1.6) and takes (-4, 1) to (-3.68, -0.6); step 2 is 0.6 times step 1 minus 0.08 times the gradient (-3.68, -12), which gives (0.4864, 0); in the w2 direction the inertia of -0.96 and the gradient pull of +0.96 cancel exactly. The figure is the table of the first three steps. The next page asks what this formula computes once unrolled.

steps.label: Why it works
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page worked out the first two steps by hand, where the two pulls on w2 cancelled. This page unrolls the update over many steps: momentum is an exponentially weighted average of past gradients; the newest gradient weighs most and every older one is multiplied by alpha once more, and the last term, alpha to the T times the initial update, is near zero after a few steps. When the direction is steady, meaning a flat surface and an almost unchanging gradient, the total weight is 1 plus alpha plus alpha squared and so on, which equals 1 over 1 minus alpha: 2.5 times for alpha 0.6 and 5 times for alpha 0.8, which a program confirmed with a fixed gradient over 80 steps. When the gradient alternates in sign the weighted average cancels it. One mechanism is fast where it can be and steady where it must be. The next page runs it for real.

steps.label: Two paths
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said momentum is an exponentially weighted average of past gradients that enlarges the step when the direction is steady and cancels when the sign flips. This page runs it for real: the same start and the same learning rate 0.08, plain gradient descent takes 100 steps and momentum with alpha 0.6 takes only 28. The red path swings up and down along w2 many times while the green one shrinks the swing faster and also moves faster along w1. The price is one more stored array for the previous update and one more alpha to tune. The next page asks whether a larger alpha is always better.

steps.label: The best α
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page used alpha 0.6, turning 100 steps into 28. This page asks whether a larger alpha is always better. With the same learning rate 0.08, alpha equal to 0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9 and 0.95 needs 100, 65, 36, 28, 44, 63, 137 and 247 steps. The fastest is near 0.6; with alpha at 0.9 or above it is even slower than no momentum, because too much inertia overshoots the valley floor and rocks like a pendulum before it stops. In practice 0.1 to 0.8 is common, the best value depends on the problem and must be tried, and the source reports speed-ups of 2 times or more. The next page asks whether the learning rate itself can adjust on its own.

steps.label: Adaptive rate
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the alpha of momentum must be tried to find its best value and the learning rate mu is the same. This page lets mu adjust itself: compare the cost J before and after a step, multiply mu by 1.05 if the ratio is below 1, by 0.7 if it is above 1.04 and keep it otherwise; these are the source's typical values and the rule is asymmetric, slow to speed up and quick to brake. When the cost rises this example rejects the step and zeroes the momentum. Results: starting from mu 0.02, plain needs 411 steps and the adaptive run only 61; starting from 0.12, plain blows up while the adaptive run rejects 12 steps and converges in 95. But from 0.08, which is already near the best, the adaptive run needs 93 steps, hardly better than plain 100. The next page asks whether we can estimate the valley floor directly instead of tuning the step.

steps.label: quickprop
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the adaptive learning rate watches the ratio of the cost before and after, yet each step still uses only the slope. This page asks whether two successive slopes can estimate the valley floor directly. That is quickprop: treat every weight as independent, draw a line through the last two slopes, estimate the bottom of the parabola and jump there, with a growth of at most 1.75 per step. Look at w2: step 1 is an ordinary step from 1 to -0.6 and the slope goes from 20 to -12; alpha is -12 over 20 plus 12, which is -0.375, and the update is -0.375 times -1.6, which is +0.6, step 2 lands exactly on 0; $w_1$ is handled the same way but its growth is capped at 1.75. The five step counts are in the figure: 411, 61, 100, 28 and 5. But every slice of this example is exactly a parabola, ideal for quickprop; every speed-up costs extra complexity. The next extension page relates it to Newton's method.

steps.label: Extension: Newton
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said quickprop estimates the valley floor of each weight and jumps there. This extension asks how that relates to Newton's method. Newton's method uses the curvature, the Hessian matrix, to compute the valley floor directly, the update being minus the inverse of H times the gradient, and a quadratic is solved in one step: here H is the diagonal matrix (1, 20), the update is exactly minus w and it reaches the origin in one step; the price is computing, storing and inverting the Hessian. quickprop can be seen as a one-dimensional Newton method per weight that estimates the curvature from two slopes. The source also lists conjugate gradient, the Newton family, Kalman filtering and Levenberg–Marquardt, most needing Hessian elements; and delta-delta and delta-bar-delta give every weight its own learning rate, growing it when the gradient keeps its sign and shrinking it when the sign flips. The next page poses a momentum exercise.

steps.label: Extension: practice
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said each weight's update rule can be rewritten on its own. This page poses the exercise: the same valley, learning rate 0.08 and alpha 0.6. After step 2 w is (-3.1936, -0.6) and the update of step 2 is (0.4864, 0). Question 1: what is the gradient here? The hint is w1 and 20 times w2. Question 2: what are the update and the new w after step 3? The update is 0.6 times the step-2 update minus 0.08 times the gradient. The figure lists the numbers of the first two steps. Work it out first, then see the next page.

steps.label: Extension: solution
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page posed the exercise and this page is the complete solution. Question 1: after step 2, w is (-3.1936, -0.6) and the gradient is w1 and 20 times w2, that is (-3.1936, -12). Question 2: the step-3 update is 0.6 times (0.4864, 0) minus 0.08 times (-3.1936, -12), which gives (0.54733, 0.96); the new w is (-2.6463, 0.36). Check: in step 2 the two pulls on w2 cancelled and w2 did not move, so this step the inertia in w2 is 0 and the whole 0.96 of the gradient part becomes displacement; the next gradient is +7.2 and the inertia will cancel part of it again. That finishes the acceleration methods.

metadata.title: Pattern Recognition, Chapter 4, KP08: speeding up backpropagation (momentum, adaptive learning rate, quickprop) (undergraduate, self-study)
